extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (also useful to patent practitioners)
extracted.subtask_short: SME analysis for nature-based patent claims
extracted.subtask_description: A step-by-step worksheet for performing 35 U.S.C. §101 subject-matter eligibility (SME) analysis on claims that involve nature-based products, following the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance and July 2015 Update. It guides claim construction (BRI), Step 1 statutory-category determination, Step 2A identification of judicial exceptions (product of nature, law of nature, natural phenomenon, abstract idea), and Step 2B assessment of whether the claim amounts to 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify invention and establish broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review the disclosure to identify what applicant considers as the invention. (MPEP 2103(I)). This can be a brief description and should not merely reproduce the claim. The take away is the focus of the invention (example: diagnosing julitis based on presence of JUL-1 in plasma).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the disclosure to state briefly what applicant invented; do not just copy claim language. Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim before proceeding with Steps 1 and 2. Use a separate worksheet for each claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory category check (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the claimed invention fall within one of the four statutory categories of invention (process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter) (Step 1)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose A (yes — continue SME analysis) or B (no — make a rejection for non-statutory subject matter using Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01). If an amendment could put the claim in a statutory category, it is recommended to continue the analysis under that assumption and document the assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is claim directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A)?
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the claim directed to a product of nature, a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea (judicially recognized exceptions)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not directed to an exception (A), conclude SME analysis. If eligibility is self-evident (B), a streamlined analysis may be used. If yes (C), proceed to identify the particular exception(s) and apply the applicable tests (e.g., markedly different characteristics for products of nature). Assistance can be obtained from the case law chart and the 2014/2015 Guidance materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-of-nature — markedly different characteristics analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is 'directed' to a product of nature exception when the claim recites a nature-based product limitation that does not exhibit markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the markedly different characteristics analysis only to the nature-based product limitations in the claim. Non-limiting examples of characteristics considered include: biological or pharmacological functions or activities; chemical and physical properties; phenotype (functional and structural characteristics); and structure and form (chemical, genetic or physical). Document the claimed limitation(s), the closest naturally occurring counterpart, and whether the claimed product exhibits markedly different characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process claims and the markedly different analysis exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Note that a process claim is not subject to the markedly different characteristics analysis for nature-based products used in the process, except where the process claim has no substantive difference from a product claim (e.g., 'a method of providing an apple').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not perform the product-of-nature markedly-different analysis on nature-based materials merely recited as part of a process claim unless the process claim is substantively equivalent to a product claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify other judicial exceptions (law of nature, natural phenomenon, abstract idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if not product-of-nature, a claim may recite a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea; identify the limitation(s) that align with judicial exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstract ideas include fundamental economic practices, certain methods of organizing human activity, ideas themselves, or mathematical relationships/formulae. Laws of nature and natural phenomena include naturally occurring principles or substances. For life-science examples, identify correlations/relationships (e.g., correlation between a biomarker and disease) and mental steps as potential exceptions (cases: Mayo, Ambry Genetics, Grams).

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis when eligibility is self-evident
rubrics_metrics.description: When eligibility is self-evident and the claim clearly does not attempt to tie up an exception, a streamlined analysis is appropriate and a full eligibility analysis is not needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to training slides for examples. If using the streamlined approach, conclude SME analysis and continue with other patentability requirements; document the rationale if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: If claim directed to a nature-based product: identify limitation(s), closest natural counterpart, and compare
rubrics_metrics.description: For nature-based product limitations, (a) identify the limitation(s) in the claim that set forth or describe a nature-based product; (b) identify the closest naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state; (c) compare the claimed product to its counterpart to determine whether it exhibits markedly different characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete all of (a), (b) and (c). Based on the comparison, choose (i) the product exhibits markedly different characteristics (not a product-of-nature exception) or (ii) it lacks markedly different characteristics (is a product-of-nature exception). Provide factual support for the comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: If claim recites abstract idea/law of nature: identify limitation(s) and explain why they are exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the claim limitations that recite the exception and explain why those recited subject matters are judicial exceptions (for example, correlations or mental steps).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how the limitation maps to case law examples (e.g., correlation = law of nature as in Mayo; mental comparison/diagnosis = abstract idea as in Ambry/Grams). Note that judicial exceptions need not be old or long-prevalent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Are there additional elements beyond the exception (Step 2B — presence of additional elements)?
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim includes any features/limitations/steps beyond the identified exception(s). If the claim is a product composed of components not occurring together in nature, treat each component as an additional element relative to the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose 1 (no additional elements — make §101 rejection and consider suggesting elements to applicant) or 2 (yes — list the additional elements and continue to evaluate their significance). If suggesting claim amendments, identify elements in the disclosure that could be added.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate significance of additional elements — search for an 'inventive concept' (Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify whether additional elements, individually or in combination, result in the claim amounting to significantly more than the judicial exception (i.e., whether they show an 'inventive concept').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the additional elements individually and in combination, and evaluate relative to what applicant invented. Reasons supporting significance can include one or more of the following: improves another technology or technical field; improves the functioning of a computer itself; applies the exception with or by use of a particular machine (not a generic computer performing generic functions); effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; adds a specific limitation other than what is well-understood, routine and conventional; adds unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application (not insignificant extrasolution activity such as mere data gathering); adds meaningful limitations more than generally linking use of the exception to a particular technological environment. Avoid counting as significant: generic computer functions, mere instructions to 'apply' the exception, or mere data gathering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination-of-elements analysis (conjunction may produce 'significantly more')
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if individual additional elements are conventional, their combination may result in significantly more than the exception (see Diamond v. Diehr).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the additional elements 'act in concert' to improve a technical field, integrate the exception into a practical application, or otherwise yield more than the sum of conventional parts. Provide reasoning showing how the combination improves diagnosis/treatment/accuracy or another technical outcome where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of well-understood, routine and conventional elements is not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of one or some well-understood, routine and conventional elements in a claim does not alone confer or preclude eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that such elements, especially when recited at a high level of generality (e.g., 'obtaining a sample'), may amount to insignificant pre-solution activity; however, they must be weighed in the context of the entire claim and in view of the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraphs and sample Office Action wording for §101 rejections and eligible findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015 (and 7.05.01 where noted) for making §101 rejections or sample eligible findings. The worksheet gives example language for a §101 rejection explaining why a claim is directed to a judicial exception and lacks significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making a rejection, include: identification of the exception (e.g., diagnosing when presence of JUL-1 is detected), explanation linking to case law (Mayo, Ambry, Grams), why additional elements are routine or mere data gathering, and why combination adds no meaningful limitations. When concluding eligibility, explicit explanation is not required in Office action unless clarification would benefit the record, but notes/examples of eligible claim reasoning are provided in the worksheet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggest claim amendments from disclosure to attempt to confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify elements in the disclosure that could be added to claims to make them eligible (e.g., a specific anti-JUL-1 antibody 'mAb-D33' or a type of antibody not routinely used to detect human proteins).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider adding unconventional or non-routine features (specific antibodies, particular machines, transformations, specific treatment steps) and document examples. Note that multiple other limitations might also render the claim eligible; list candidate limitations for applicant to consider.
